name: Semmelweis and the two wards
scope: The doctor who found the killer in his own hands. T1: at the Vienna General Hospital two maternity clinics sat one door apart, and women BEGGED to be sent to the midwives' side — some deliberately gave birth in the street and then came in, because street births survived better than the doctors' ward. T2a: the numbers behind the begging — 1841-46 the First Clinic (physicians and medical students) averaged about 10% maternal deaths from childbed fever; the Second Clinic (student midwives) under 4%; in 1846 it was 11.4% vs 2.8%. T2b: the clue was a colleague's death — in 1847 Jakob Kolletschka was nicked by a student's scalpel during a post-mortem and died with the SAME internal findings Semmelweis kept seeing in dead mothers. T3a: the one difference between the wards was the morning routine — the doctors came to the delivery beds straight from the dissection room; the midwives never touched a corpse. T3b: mid-May 1847 he ordered every hand scrubbed in chlorinated lime before examinations; April's 18.3% fell to 2.2% in June, 1.2% in July, 1.9% in August. T3c: he had the EFFECT without the MECHANISM — he could only call it 'cadaverous particles'; bacteria were three decades away, and his critics used that gap against him. T4a: he was not first — Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr told American doctors the same thing in 1843 ('The Contagiousness of Puerperal Fever') and Charles Meigs answered that doctors are gentlemen and gentlemen's hands are clean. T4b: Vienna froze him out — Johann Klein passed him over for Carl Braun and he left for Pest. T4c: his 1861 book Die Ätiologie... landed badly, and he followed it with open letters calling his opponents murderers; being right did not make him persuasive. T5a: on 30 July 1865 Ferdinand von Hebra lured him to a Viennese asylum, where guards beat him and put him in a straitjacket; he was dead in two weeks, aged 47. T5b: the autopsy said pyaemia from a gangrenous wound on his right hand — blood poisoning, the same family of infection that killed his patients. T5c: vindication came from other men's mechanism — Pasteur's germs and Lister's carbolic supplied the reason his rule worked; Budapest's medical university now carries his name, and 'Semmelweis reflex' is the phrase for reflexively rejecting evidence that contradicts the reigning paradigm.

framing_note: DISCOVERY/FIGURE ladder and the flagship REVERSAL of this sub-strand. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (women giving birth in the street rather than enter the doctors' ward) — key the ACT, never a date. ACCURACY RAIL (the one that matters): Semmelweis did NOT know about bacteria and never said 'germs' — his term was cadaverous/decaying animal-organic particles; do not backdate germ theory into his mouth, and do not repeat the popular embellishment that he cut himself on a cadaver on purpose (the documented cause is pyaemia from a gangrenous hand wound after the asylum beating). Second rail: the mortality fall is real and huge, but quote the monthly figures, not a rounded legend. Distractor mine is exceptional here — the Vienna faculty's own live explanations: miasma/bad air in the ward, overcrowding, poor ventilation, the priest's bell frightening the women, 'wounded modesty' at being examined by men, the delivery position, cold weather, diet. All were respectable, all were wrong, none are jokes. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem contain 'infection carried on unwashed hands' before asking what Semmelweis found — describe only what he SAW (two wards, tripled deaths, a colleague dead from a scalpel nick) and make the cause recalled knowledge. Balance rung T4c honestly: he was right AND he was a ruinous advocate — the bank honours the dissenter without pretending the establishment had no reason to bristle.

name: John Snow and the Broad Street pump
scope: How a map beat bad air. T1: on 31 August 1854 cholera erupted in Soho and 127 people died within three days on and around one street; Snow marked every death at its address on a street map and the marks piled up around ONE thing — the public water pump on Broad Street. T2a: the first anomaly that fitted water — the Lion Brewery stood in the middle of the deaths and its workers did not get cholera; they had their own well and a daily beer ration and never drank from the pump. T2b: the second anomaly — the Poland Street workhouse held over 500 inmates packed together in the worst of it and lost only a handful; it had its own piped supply. T3a: the death that broke miasma — Susannah Eley, a widow living miles away in Hampstead, so liked the taste of Broad Street water that she had it carted to her; she died of cholera, and so did a niece visiting from Islington. Bad air does not travel in a cart. T3b: the handle came off on 8 September 1854 after Snow argued the parish board into it. T3c: Snow then argued against his own best story — he wrote that deaths were already falling before the handle was removed, because most of the neighbourhood had fled, so he could not claim the removal ended the outbreak. T4a: the source was found by a man trying to REFUTE him — curate Henry Whitehead traced the index case to baby Frances Lewis, whose mother had rinsed the soiled nappies into a cesspit dug three feet from the well. T4b: the map's hidden method — Snow shaded the zone in which Broad Street was the nearest pump BY WALKING DISTANCE through the alleys, not straight-line distance, and the deaths sat inside that line. T4c: the real proof was not Soho at all but the 'Grand Experiment' in south London: two companies piped water into the same streets, sometimes to neighbouring houses; Lambeth had moved its intake upriver in 1852, Southwark & Vauxhall still drew from the sewage-fouled Thames — and cholera deaths ran about fourteen times higher in the Southwark & Vauxhall houses. T5a: the General Board of Health's inquiry rejected him and blamed miasma; faecal-oral transmission was unthinkable in polite Victorian company. T5b: the microbe already existed on paper — Filippo Pacini described the comma-shaped cholera vibrio in Florence in that same year, 1854, and was ignored; Koch re-found it in Egypt and India in 1883-84. T5c: the convert — William Farr, the government statistician who had backed miasma with a real correlation between cholera and low elevation, used Snow's own method in the 1866 East London outbreak and traced it to one company's reservoir. Snow had died in 1858 without seeing it.

framing_note: DISCOVERY ladder with a method spine — the birth of epidemiology. Dinner-test payoff: T3a, the Hampstead widow who had the water delivered and died of it (bad air cannot ride a cart) — the single most transferable rung in the sub-strand. ACCURACY RAIL: do NOT teach the schoolbook version 'Snow removed the handle and the epidemic stopped'. Snow himself said deaths were already falling; the handle is the famous image, the MAP and the two-water-company comparison are the actual evidence. Second rail: Snow never saw a cholera germ and never claimed to — he inferred a self-multiplying poison swallowed in water; keep the microbe out of his mouth (that is Pacini's and Koch's rung). Distractor mine: the era's genuinely live explanations — miasma from the Thames and the graveyards, sewer gas, night air, elevation above the river (Farr's real, reproducible correlation), intemperance and 'moral character', contagion by touch, the rival pumps. LANE BORDER: the geography bank already tours London, Soho and the Thames — science keys the METHOD (dot map, nearest-pump-by-walking-distance shading, natural experiment) and the reasoning, never a place-tour or a street-name recall. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: no stem may say 'contaminated drinking water' before asking what Snow concluded; give only the pattern he saw.
history_overlap: geography bank: London / the Thames / Soho as places and possibly 'famous maps' — this ladder must key the METHOD and evidence, not the place. history bank: Victorian London public health and the sanitary reforms may already carry the Great Stink and Bazalgette (see the miasma ladder, which owns that fact here).

name: Pasteur's swan-neck flask
scope: The most elegant control ever blown in glass. T1: Pasteur boiled meat broth in a flask whose neck he had drawn out into a long S-curve and then left it OPEN to the room — air flowed in and out freely, dust settled in the bend, and the broth stayed clear for months while an ordinary open flask clouded in a day. T2a: the one-move control that ends the argument — tip the flask so the broth runs into the curve and pour it back, and the same broth in the same air clouds within a day. One variable changed, everything else held. T2b: the shape was aimed at a specific objection — opponents said boiling and sealing destroyed a 'vital force' in the air that living things needed; the swan neck admitted the air and excluded the dust, answering the objection instead of dodging it. T3a: he took the argument up a mountain — sealed sterile flasks snapped open and resealed in the countryside, on a hill in the Jura, and out on the Mer de Glace glacier: the higher and cleaner the air, the fewer flasks spoiled. Life was in the DUST, not in the air. T3b: the French Academy of Sciences had offered a prize for settling the question; Pasteur took it in 1862. T4a: the opponent was not a crank — Félix Pouchet got real growth in flasks that should have stayed sterile, using hay infusions, and reported it honestly. Pasteur's conclusion was right and Pouchet's data were also real. T4b: the resolution came later and vindicated both — hay carries heat-resistant bacterial SPORES that survive ordinary boiling; John Tyndall worked it out and invented repeated heating to kill them, and Ferdinand Cohn described the spores. T4c: the honest caveat on how the fight was won — the Academy's judging commissions were unsympathetic and Pouchet withdrew rather than be judged; the right answer partly won on politics, which is not the same as winning on evidence. T5a: the ancestors — Francesco Redi in 1668 covered meat with fine gauze and got maggots on the CLOTH and none on the meat; flies, not rot, made maggots. That killed spontaneous generation for big animals but not for the invisible. T5b: John Needham's boiled sealed broths clouded and Lazzaro Spallanzani's, boiled longer in glass he melted shut, did not — and Spallanzani was answered with 'you destroyed the vital force', which is exactly the hole the swan neck plugged. T5c: what the flask bought — if life does not arise in broth, then souring, rotting and wound infection all come from something that ARRIVES, and the flask becomes the ancestor of the sterile operating theatre and the canning jar.

framing_note: DISCOVERY ladder built around a CONTROL — the sub-strand's method backbone. Dinner-test payoff: T2a (tilt the flask and the same broth clouds overnight) — this is the rung a kid can retell and half-imagine building. ACCURACY RAIL: the swan-neck flask is NOT sealed; the whole force of the experiment is that it is open to the air. Any stem or answer that says 'sealed' breaks the logic. Second rail: Pasteur did not prove life never arose anywhere ever — he proved it does not arise in boiled broth under these conditions; say it that precisely, and keep the origin-of-life question out (that is a MYSTERY the bank does not pretend is closed). Distractor mine: spontaneous generation itself, the 'vital force'/vitalism, miasma, 'the air itself carries life', Lamarckism, Needham's leaky seals. LANE BORDER: the cooking bank owns pasteurised milk and wine spoilage; science owns the flask and the control. Also keep philosophy's Popper seminar out — this ladder shows falsification as WORKING PRACTICE (what a good control physically looks like), not as an epistemology lecture. T4a-T4c are the honesty spine: an honest opponent with real data, an anomaly that turned out to have a germ explanation, and a victory that was partly political.
history_overlap: cooking bank: pasteurisation of milk/wine and the souring of food — this ladder must not restage 'why milk is heated'; it owns only the flask control and the spontaneous-generation kill.

name: Koch's four-step test for a killer
scope: CONCEPT ladder: how you PROVE a particular germ causes a particular disease, deepened across the cases that forged the checklist. T2a: the problem the rule exists to solve — Koch found rod-shaped bacteria in the blood of every animal dead of anthrax, but a microbe in a corpse can be the cause, a harmless passenger, or a scavenger that arrived after death; being present is not being guilty. T2b: the chain he actually ran, in a converted room in his house in Wollstein with no laboratory and no colleagues — grow the anthrax rods outside any animal, inject them into a healthy mouse, watch that mouse die of anthrax, then find the same rods in it. Find it, grow it pure, give the disease, get it back. T3a: the MECHANISM rung — Koch watched the rods form tough oval spores that survived drying for years, which finally explained the farmers' 'cursed fields' that killed livestock decades after an infected animal was buried there. T3b: the gatekeeper — Ferdinand Cohn in Breslau made the unknown country doctor demonstrate the whole thing at the bench for three days before he would believe it, then published him; Koch's 1877 work produced the first photograph of a bacterium. T4a: the checklist needed a surface — gelatine melted at body heat and potato slices grew the wrong things, until Fanny Hesse, an American-born wife of one of Koch's assistants, suggested the agar she used for jellies at home; agar stays firm at 37 degrees. T4b: the dish — Julius Petri published a 'minor modification' in 1887, using the flat glass dish itself with a loose lid instead of Koch's bell-jar arrangement; the most-used object in biology is named for one assistant's tweak. T4c: 24 March 1882 in Berlin — Koch laid out the tuberculosis bacillus before the Physiological Society and the room gave him nothing: no applause, no questions. Paul Ehrlich, sitting there, later called it the greatest scientific experience of his life. T5a: the rule Koch himself broke — he found people carrying cholera, and later typhoid, who never fell ill, which contradicts step one ('absent in the healthy'); he said so publicly and loosened his own postulate. T5b: where the checklist cannot reach — viruses will not grow in pure culture because they need living cells, some bacteria will not culture at all, and prions are not organisms; modern causal argument leans on Bradford Hill's criteria alongside Koch's. T5c: the author of the rules broke them himself — in August 1890 Koch announced tuberculin as a tuberculosis remedy before it was proven; it did not cure, patients died, and Virchow's autopsies said so. He took the 1905 Nobel for tuberculosis anyway.

framing_note: CONCEPT/THEME ladder — the analytic backbone of this sub-strand, which is why it carries native T4/T5. Dinner-test payoff: T3a (spores explain why a field could still kill cattle decades after a burial) — vivid, mechanistic, and it makes a kid look at soil differently. ACCURACY RAIL: teach the four steps in plain words BEFORE any rung tests them, and never test them as a numbered recital — every rung must run the logic on a real case (anthrax, TB, cholera, a carrier). Do not present the postulates as a still-binding law: Koch loosened postulate one himself, and viruses break postulate two by definition; the honest framing is 'the first serious checklist for causation, and here is where it leaks'. Distractor mine: miasma, spontaneous generation, 'bad blood'/humoral explanations, hereditary tuberculosis (the reigning theory before Koch — respectable and wrong), Pettenkofer's ground-water theory, and Pacini's real-but-unnoticed 1854 vibrio. LANE BORDERS: the animal bank owns anthrax as a livestock disease and sheep as creatures — science owns the proof procedure; the cooking bank owns agar and gelatine as kitchen ingredients — here agar appears only as the technical fix that made pure culture possible. T5c is not a takedown but the bank's own virtue applied to a hero: the man who wrote the rules for proof announced a cure before proving it.
history_overlap: animal bank: anthrax in cattle and sheep as an animal disease. cooking bank: agar and gelatine as setting agents. Both appear here only as instruments of the causation proof, never as the subject.

name: Miasma, the honest wrong consensus
scope: CONCEPT ladder: the two-thousand-year-old theory that was reasonable, useful, and wrong — and what finally settled it. T2a: one disease still carries the dead theory's name — 'malaria' is Italian for bad air, named for the marsh vapours that were blamed for it, and it turned out to ride a mosquito. The word is a fossil of a wrong idea. T2b: why miasma was not stupid — disease genuinely did cluster where the stink was, around open sewers, marshes and slums. The correlation was real; the causal arrow pointed the wrong way. T3a: Edwin Chadwick's 1842 Sanitary Report ran on the flat claim that all smell is disease — and it produced drains, street cleaning and the Public Health Act. A wrong theory prescribing right actions. T3b: the Great Stink of 1858 — the Thames reeked so badly that Parliament hung lime-soaked curtains at the windows and then voted the money for Joseph Bazalgette's intercepting sewers, which were built to carry away the SMELL and happened to carry away the cholera. T3c: the detail that proves the point — London's last major cholera outbreak, in 1866, struck the East End district that was not yet connected to the new sewers. T4a: Florence Nightingale was a committed miasmatist who distrusted contagion, and her fresh air, open windows and scrubbing saved lives anyway; holding the wrong mechanism did not make her useless. T4b: William Farr, the government's statistician, found that cholera deaths fell steadily with height above the Thames — a strong, real, reproducible correlation that fitted miasma beautifully and was actually tracking which water company served which ground. A perfect example of a genuine pattern supporting a false cause. T5a: the mirror-image self-experiment — on 7 October 1892 Max von Pettenkofer, Munich's great sanitary reformer, drank a broth of cholera bacteria in front of witnesses to disprove Koch, and did not get cholera. A brave maverick testing his own claim on his own body, and getting a misleading answer. T5b: how that result reads now — likely partial immunity from an earlier mild infection, plus dose and the bicarbonate he swallowed to protect the bacteria from his stomach acid; the lesson is that one dramatic self-experiment is not evidence, because Barry Marshall's beaker and Pettenkofer's beaker looked identical from the outside and only one man was right. T5c: what actually ended the argument was not eloquence but tests that could go either way — Snow comparing two water companies house by house, and Koch growing the comma bacillus in pure culture. Plausibility lost to procedure.

Drop what will not verify.
framing_note: CONCEPT/THEME ladder and the single richest DISTRACTOR MINE in the sub-strand — every other ladder here draws its wrong options from this one, so the bank owes miasma a fair hearing rather than a laugh. Dinner-test payoff: T5a, Pettenkofer drinking the cholera broth — because it is the exact mirror of Barry Marshall's beaker and it forces the harder lesson. VOICE RULE: present miasma as respectable, reasonable and wrong. Never sneer; a kid who learns to sneer at past scientists has learned the opposite of the intended virtue. The stance the bank IS taking here is the one it takes everywhere: consensus is not evidence — but the corollary, taught just as hard at T5b, is that the lone dissenter is not evidence either. Pettenkofer was brave, sincere, self-testing, and wrong. ACCURACY RAIL: do not say miasma 'accidentally' worked — it worked because filth and germs genuinely co-occur, so the interventions hit the real cause by a different route; that is the whole insight of the ladder. Second rail: never let a distractor here secretly be the truth, and never imply germ theory arrived in a single moment. Distractors within this ladder: contagionism, humoral theory, zymotic theory (Farr's own term), Pettenkofer's X-Y-Z ground-water theory, telluric emanations. LANE BORDER: the geography bank owns the Thames and London's sewers as places; history owns Parliament and the Great Stink as a political episode — science keeps the wedge between correlation and cause.
history_overlap: history bank: the Great Stink of 1858 and Parliament's response, and Victorian sanitary reform as a political episode. geography bank: the Thames and London's sewer system as a place-anchored engineering feature. Science keys only the epistemics — why a wrong theory produced right actions and what finally settled it.

name: Pouilly-le-Fort: the test he announced in advance
scope: The public experiment with a control group, staged by a sceptic. T1: in May 1881, on a farm at Pouilly-le-Fort outside Melun, Pasteur did the thing that makes a claim testable — he wrote down, in advance and in public, exactly what would happen to each animal and on what day, then let a hostile press come and watch. T2a: the design — two matched groups; half the animals got his anthrax vaccine on 5 and 17 May, half got nothing, and then EVERY animal, vaccinated and not, was injected with live anthrax on 31 May. The trial ran on 58 sheep, 2 goats and 10 cattle, not the tidy 25-and-25 of the legend. T2b: on 2 June the crowd walked into the field and found every unvaccinated sheep dead or dying and every vaccinated one on its feet and grazing. T3a: why the unvaccinated half is the whole trick — anthrax does not kill every exposed animal every time, so 'my vaccinated sheep lived' would have proved nothing at all without a control group dying beside them. T3b: the trap was set BY THE SCEPTIC — the veterinarian Hippolyte Rossignol, who thought Pasteur a charlatan, proposed the trial and provided the farm, expecting a public humiliation. T4: the MECHANISM behind it, found by accident — attenuation. Pasteur's assistants had left a chicken-cholera culture sitting over a holiday; the stale culture failed to kill the chickens, and those same chickens then survived a fresh, lethal dose. A weakened germ teaches the body the enemy's face without the fight. T5a: the honest caveat — Pasteur told the world he had used his own oxygen-attenuated live vaccine, but his laboratory notebooks, opened to scholars a century later and analysed by Gerald Geison, show the Pouilly-le-Fort doses were made by Charles Chamberland's potassium-dichromate method, essentially the approach of his rival Jean-Joseph-Henri Toussaint. The result was genuine; the story of how he got it was not. T5b: the word itself is a courtesy — Pasteur chose to call these preparations 'vaccines', from the Latin vacca, cow, in honour of Edward Jenner's cowpox, and the name spread to the whole field.

framing_note: DISCOVERY ladder that doubles as the sub-strand's CONTROL-GROUP exemplar. Dinner-test payoff: T3b — the sceptic designed the test, which is the most useful thing a kid can learn about how science settles arguments. ACCURACY RAIL: correct the famous 25-and-25 to the documented 58 sheep, 2 goats and 10 cattle with half vaccinated; the legend is tidier than the truth and the bank tells the truth. Second rail: T5a must be stated as Geison's notebook finding, not as a rumour, and must not be turned into 'Pasteur was a fraud' — the trial result stands; what he misreported was the preparation. LANE BORDER (important): this is a nineteenth-century DISCOVERY ladder, not the bank's vaccine-stance ladder. Keep modern vaccine policy, schedules and controversy entirely out of it; the stance ladder lives elsewhere in the bank and this one must not be warped to carry it. Distractor mine: spontaneous generation, miasma, Toussaint's killed vaccine, Jenner's cowpox, 'the sheep happened to be resistant', Koch's rival German laboratory. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem say 'the vaccinated sheep survived' before asking what the trial demonstrated.
history_overlap: animal bank: sheep and cattle as livestock and anthrax as an animal disease. This ladder owns only the trial design and its outcome, never the animals themselves.

name: Rabies and the boy Pasteur was not allowed to inject
scope: Beating an enemy nobody could see. T1: on 6 July 1885 a nine-year-old from Alsace, Joseph Meister, arrived in Paris badly mauled by a rabid dog two days earlier — and the man whose treatment saved him never touched the syringe. Pasteur held no medical licence and was legally barred from injecting a patient, so the physician Jacques-Joseph Grancher gave all thirteen injections over ten days while Pasteur watched. T2: what was actually in those syringes — dried spinal cord from rabbits that had died of rabies, dried for fewer and fewer days as the course went on, so every dose was a little stronger than the last. A ladder of rising virulence, climbed faster than the disease. T3: why treating someone AFTER the bite can work at all — the rabies agent creeps slowly along the nerves toward the brain, which buys weeks; a vaccine started after exposure can still win the race. That race is still how a bitten person is treated today. T4a: the enemy was invisible in a way even a microscope could not fix — Pasteur never saw the rabies agent, could not grow it on any plate or in any broth, and had no concept of a virus. He kept it alive only by passing it through rabbit after rabbit, and defeated something he could not culture, stain or photograph. T4b: the second patient made it famous — Jean-Baptiste Jupille, a fifteen-year-old shepherd who fought off a rabid dog with his bare hands and his whip to protect younger children and was bitten doing it; he was treated and lived, and his statue stands at the Institut Pasteur. T5a: the honest caveat, opened a century later — Gerald Geison's reading of Pasteur's sealed notebooks showed he had tested this exact protocol on eleven dogs, not the fifty he implied, and had already tried a rabies treatment on two people before Meister; one of them died. He gambled harder than he told anyone. T5b: a famous story told AS a story — the legend that Meister, by then the Institute's caretaker, shot himself in June 1940 rather than open Pasteur's crypt for German soldiers. He did die by his own hand on 24 June 1940, but a contemporary account and his granddaughter's testimony describe a man who had sent his family away, stayed to guard the Institute, and killed himself believing wrongly that they had been captured. T5c: what one boy's survival built — public subscriptions arrived from all over the world and paid for the Institut Pasteur, opened in 1888.

ACCURACY RAIL: rabies is caused by a VIRUS, and Pasteur did not know that, never saw it, and never claimed to have isolated it — do not credit him with discovering the virus, and do not let a distractor imply he did. Never present the crypt version as fact. name: Lister's carbolic and the coat he stopped wearing
scope: The surgeon who believed in killers he could not see. T1: in the 1860s a hospital operation was more dangerous than the injury that caused it, and a surgeon's blood-stiffened frock coat was a badge of experience he was proud of; nearly half of amputation patients died afterwards of 'hospital gangrene' or 'ward fever'. Lister's answer came from an unglamorous place: carbolic acid, the chemical already being used to treat stinking sewage. T2: the first case — in August 1865 an eleven-year-old, James Greenlees, came in with his leg broken by a cart wheel and the bone through the skin. A compound fracture then usually meant amputation or death; Lister dressed it with carbolic, the wound did not go bad, and the boy walked out on both legs. T3: what Lister had that Semmelweis did not was a MECHANISM. Reading Pasteur on fermentation, he concluded that wound putrefaction was living organisms arriving from outside — so he treated not only the wound but the instruments, the sutures, the surgeon's hands and the dressings. Theory told him what to do next. T4a: the numbers he published — mortality on his male accident ward fell from roughly 46 per cent before antisepsis to about 15 per cent after, and he set the argument out in The Lancet in 1867 as 'On the Antiseptic Principle in the Practice of Surgery'. T4b: the resistance sounded practical, not stupid — surgeons pointed out that nobody could see these organisms, the carbolic burned patients and cracked the surgeon's hands, and the older obstetrician James Young Simpson attacked him in print; French, German and American surgeons took it up faster than the London hospitals did. T5a: the self-correction that is the best thing about him — the carbolic steam spray, his most famous and most photographed apparatus, was the piece Lister himself later abandoned, having concluded that germs floating in the air mattered far less than what actually touched the wound. He dropped his own signature invention. T5b: the shift he started ran past him — from ANTIseptic (kill what is in the wound) to ASEPTIC (never let it in): steam-sterilised instruments, gowns, caps, and rubber gloves, which William Halsted first ordered for a scrub nurse whose hands the antiseptics had ruined. T5c: the odd afterlife of the name — a St Louis chemist named an antiseptic after him in 1879; Listerine was sold first as a surgical antiseptic and a floor cleaner, and only decades later as mouthwash.

framing_note: DISCOVERY/FIGURE ladder; the companion piece to Semmelweis — same enemy, better luck, because Lister had Pasteur's mechanism and a gentler manner. Dinner-test payoff: T5c (Listerine is named after a surgeon and started life as a wound antiseptic) — the rung a kid will repeat at the bathroom sink; T1's blood-stiff frock coat is the hook that makes them wince. ACCURACY RAIL: do NOT use any mocking quotation attributed to Lister's opponents unless the build can document it in a real source — several famous lines about closing windows against 'Mr Lister's germs' circulate without provenance. State the resistance in the surgeons' own reasonable terms instead (nobody could see the organisms; the carbolic genuinely injured tissue and hands). Second rail: pin the mortality percentages to Lister's own published figures with their year ranges, or state them as 'roughly' — do not invent precision. T5a is the voice-critical rung: the bank's first virtue is scepticism of your OWN claims, and Lister publicly gave up his most famous device. Distractor mine: miasma and ward air, spontaneous generation, 'laudable pus' (the genuine older doctrine that pus was a good sign of healing), cauterisation, Semmelweis's chlorinated lime as the adjacent-but-different answer.

name: Nightingale's rose diagram
scope: Data drawn as a weapon — and the honest story of what actually saved the soldiers. T2a: in the Crimean War's first winter far more British soldiers were killed by disease inside the hospital than by anything the Russians did; Nightingale's response was to DRAW it, as a circle of twelve wedges, one for each month, in which the outer blue area for preventable disease swamps the small red one for wounds. T2b: she drew it because she was arguing with ministers and a queen who would not read a table — the picture was aimed at people who could be moved by an image and not by an appendix. T3a: the honest flaw in the most famous chart in public health — every wedge has the same angle and varies in RADIUS, so the area grows as the square, and the bad months look even worse than they were. A modern statistician would reach for a plain bar chart, and a kid with graph paper can check this. T3b: what her own numbers told her afterwards — her first months of nursing did NOT bring the death rate down. T4: the cause was found by the men who arrived later — a Sanitary Commission sent out in March 1855 flushed the sewers under the Barrack Hospital and cleaned up the water supply, and the mortality collapsed after that. Nightingale worked this out from her own data and never claimed the fall as her own achievement. T5a: what she DID with the finding — she turned it on peacetime Britain, arguing that the army's own barracks at home were killing soldiers too, and got a Royal Commission and a programme of sanitary reform out of a diagram. T5b: the theory she held was the wrong one — she distrusted contagion and believed in bad air to the end of her active career, prescribing ventilation, drainage and scrubbing; only in later life did she speak of killing germs. She got the right prescription from the wrong mechanism, and the numbers, not the theory, are what she trusted.

BUILD MUST RE-CHECK GROKIPEDIA FIRST and must verify before seeding: (a) the RSS election year — sources give both 1858 and 1859, so do not build a rung that turns on it, (b) the exact wording of her 'affect thro' the Eyes' line before quoting it at all, (c) that polar-area diagrams predate her (Guerry, Playfair) so she popularised rather than invented the form.

Dinner-test payoff: T4, because it inverts the story every kid is told: Nightingale's greatest act was working out from her own numbers that her nursing was NOT what dropped the death rate. That is the discovery pattern and the self-scepticism virtue in one rung. ACCURACY RAIL: do not teach 'Nightingale's nursing halved the death rate' — the Sanitary Commission's drains and water supply did, and she is the person who established this. Second rail: no quotation unless the exact wording is documented, and no rung that turns on the disputed RSS election year (dates are banned anyway). T3a is a genuine invitation to check: radius-scaled wedges exaggerate, and a kid can redraw the same data as bars. LANE BORDER: the history bank almost certainly owns the Crimean War, Scutari and 'the Lady with the Lamp' — science must key the DIAGRAM, the flaw in it, and the causal finding, never the war narrative or a biography sketch. Distractor mine: miasma, contagionism, 'the wounds themselves', poor food, the cold, incompetent generals — all real and all argued at the time.
history_overlap: history bank: the Crimean War, Scutari, and Nightingale as 'the Lady with the Lamp' are very likely already there. This ladder must key only the statistics, the chart's design flaw, and the Sanitary Commission's causal role — no war narrative, no lamp.

name: Leeuwenhoek's animalcules
scope: The day a shopkeeper found a crowded world in a drop of water. T1: a cloth merchant in Delft with no university education and no Latin ground a bead of glass the size of a pinhead, held it to his eye, looked at water from a nearby lake, and found it swarming with things that swam. He called them dierkens — little animals. T2a: his day job put the lens in his hand: drapers used magnifying glasses to count the threads in a bolt of cloth, and he was better at making them than anyone alive. T2b: his 'microscope' is not a tube — it is a brass plate about the size of a large stamp with one tiny glass bead in it, and his best ones reached roughly 270 times magnification, sharper than any two-lens microscope of his century. T3a: the Royal Society in London could not reproduce it and doubted him outright; independent witnesses were sent to Delft and the observations were confirmed, and only then was he believed and eventually elected a Fellow. Replication, not reputation, settled it. T3b: the first picture of bacteria in history came off his own teeth — in 1683 he scraped the film from between them, saw rods, spirals and darting specks, and drew them; he also went and looked at the mouth of an old man who had never cleaned his teeth in his life. T4a: he tested on the nearest available subject: when he had violent diarrhoea he put his own stool under the lens and described the pear-shaped swimmers we now call Giardia. T4b: the secret he took to the grave — he never told anyone how he made the lenses, produced hundreds of instruments of which only about nine survive, and a 2021 neutron-tomography scan of one of them finally showed the lens was a pulled glass filament rather than the exotic technique historians had assumed. T4c: the strangest fact of all — he SAW the germs and never connected them to disease, and neither did anyone else for nearly two centuries. The evidence sat in plain view, correctly drawn and published, waiting for a theory that could use it.
source: Grokipedia checked FIRST (grokipedia.com/page/Antonie_van_Leeuwenhoek) — HTTP 403, Chrome bridge offline, unreadable; verified against en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonie_van_Leeuwenhoek (draper in Delft, own linen shop from 1654; observed moving microscopic organisms in pond water in 1674, calling them dierkens/diertjes; the letter of 9 October 1676 met scepticism and the Royal Society arranged verification through local ministers and observers in 1677; 1683 observations of bacteria from his own mouth; single-lens instruments up to about 275x; over 500 lenses, at least 25 microscopes, nine surviving; strict secrecy about construction, with a 2021 neutron-tomography study showing pulled glass filaments; no evidence he connected animalcules to disease). BUILD MUST RE-CHECK GROKIPEDIA FIRST and must verify before seeding: (a) the specific lake (commonly the Berkelse Mere), (b) whether Robert Hooke personally reproduced the sighting or whether it was other appointed witnesses — state it the way the sources support, (c) the Giardia-in-his-own-stool observation of 1681.
framing_note: DISCOVERY ladder and the sub-strand's opening move: before you can fight an invisible enemy you have to SEE it. Dinner-test payoff: T3b, the plaque scraped off his own teeth and the old man who had never cleaned his — kids find this delightful and disgusting in the right proportion, and it is the first drawing of bacteria in history. TEST-IT-YOURSELF: this is the most kid-replicable ladder here — pond water and a cheap microscope reproduce the 1674 moment exactly; frame at least one rung as that invitation. ACCURACY RAIL: Leeuwenhoek never linked animalcules to disease and had no germ theory — the ladder's payoff (T4c) is precisely that gap, so no rung and no distractor may imply he did. Second rail: he did not invent the microscope (compound instruments already existed); he made single-lens instruments that beat them. LANE BORDER: Robert Hooke's cork cells and the naming of the 'cell' belong to the bank's cell-biology strand — Hooke appears here only as part of the replication story. Distractor mine: spontaneous generation, the vital force, miasma, Hooke's Micrographia, 'he invented the microscope', 'he proved germs cause disease'.

name: The healthy carrier: Mary Mallon
scope: The enemy that rides someone who feels perfectly fine. T3: a New York cook worked for eight households in the early 1900s and typhoid broke out in seven of them, while she was never sick a day in her life; the sanitary engineer George Soper caught her by tracing her employment history from house to house, and noted she served a peach ice cream that never went near heat. T4: the mechanism that makes a healthy carrier possible — Salmonella Typhi can settle in the gallbladder and be shed in the stool for years by someone with no symptoms at all. Mallon did not believe she was the cause and refused to have her gallbladder taken out. T5: what she does to Koch's first rule — 'found in the sick and absent in the healthy' simply fails for carriers, and Koch had already run into the same wall with symptomless cholera carriers and loosened his own postulate. Mallon spent about twenty-six years in total confined on North Brother Island, where she died in 1938; up to fifty-seven cases and three deaths were traced to her, and the hard part of the story is that hundreds of other healthy carriers were identified in New York and she is the one who was locked up for life.
source: Grokipedia checked FIRST (grokipedia.com/page/Mary_Mallon) — HTTP 403, Chrome bridge offline, unreadable; verified against en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Mallon (cook for wealthy New York families; George Soper hired after the 1906 Oyster Bay outbreak, mapped her employment history, noted the ice cream with fresh peaches; eight families worked for, seven with outbreaks, twenty-six confirmed cases connected; forcibly quarantined on North Brother Island in 1907 for three years; released 19 February 1910 on an agreement to stop cooking; worked as 'Mary Brown' at Sloane Maternity Hospital; the January-February 1915 outbreak of twenty-five cases with two deaths; returned to North Brother Island March 1915 until her death 11 November 1938; up to fifty-seven cases and three confirmed deaths attributed; the gallbladder as the reservoir and her refusal of surgery) and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koch's_postulates (asymptomatic carriers of cholera and typhoid led Koch to abandon the universalist first postulate). Dinner-test payoff: T3 (seven outbreaks in eight households and she was never ill). ACCURACY RAIL: the popular nickname 'Typhoid Mary' is a period label, not a diagnosis — use her real name and let the nickname appear only as what newspapers called her; and do not imply she knew and did it deliberately, because the documented picture is a woman who genuinely did not believe the theory. TONE RULE: state the liberty cost plainly — decades of confinement for a woman who had committed no crime and felt fine — and then stop. Present, do not preach; this is not a stance ladder and must not be turned into one in either direction. Distractor mine: miasma, contaminated municipal water (the era's default and often correct explanation for typhoid), flies, milk supply, 'she had a mild case nobody noticed'. LANE BORDER: the cooking bank owns the food itself, including uncooked ice cream as a transmission route — this ladder owns the carrier mechanism and the hole it punched in Koch's first postulate.
